data.why: The app takes no file upload; a researcher only types a KIC number or picks one of four built-in demo stars, and the app itself fetches the real Kepler light curve from MAST via lightkurve at runtime — there is nothing to hand the browser as a test file.

goals: Screen a known Kepler star (e.g. KIC 11446443 / Kepler-1b) and confirm the CNN scores it above the calibrated 0.6914 threshold as a planet candidate
Enter an unfamiliar KIC number and read off the planet probability score, confidence tier, and the processed light-curve segment the CNN actually saw
Check whether a high-scoring candidate is really a planet or a false-positive eclipsing binary by running the phase-fold EB check with the star's orbital period
Probe the model's known failure modes (active/variable stars, long-period planets, low-SNR planets) using the documented demo stars and see the near-zero scores first-hand
Inspect the preprocessing pipeline output (segment selection, L2 normalisation, Gaussian smoothing) to judge whether the best-variance window actually captured a transit

review.summary: The tree accurately records what could be reached: input setup, the failed MAST fetch and the Performance/About pages, and every screen I opened matches its node. But the sandbox blocked MAST, so the tool's core job (reading the score and tier, looking at the light curve and segment the CNN saw, and running the eclipsing-binary rejection) is missing from both the tree and the features. It needs a re-run with network access, or code-sourced nodes marked unverified, before it is filed.
